summary: Training volume over the last 4 weeks has been extremely low — just 4 sessions totalling roughly 158 minutes of meaningful work — with no cycling or running recorded and swim volume far below what is needed for a 5,000m open-water race in 28 days. Wellness data paints a concerning picture: sleep is chronically short (often 3–5 hours, frequently below 4), body battery is regularly in the 10–40 range, and there are multiple near-zero days, indicating the body is carrying significant accumulated fatigue. The priority right now must be sleep and recovery first, then a careful, progressive ramp in swim volume over the next 3–4 weeks to give the Half Oceanman the best possible preparation.
suggestions: Sleep is the single biggest limiter right now — body battery is consistently below 40 and sleep duration averages under 5.5 hours; target a minimum of 7 hours per night this week before adding any training stress.

Swim volume is critically low for a 5,000m race in 28 days: prioritise getting in the water 3 times per week immediately, building toward a 2,500–3,000m continuous or near-continuous session by race week at ≤2:30/100m.

Treat the Wk12 long ride (110km, 240 min on 12 Sep) as a firm cap of 90 min / 60km given the near-zero training base — the plan's AI-adjusted Wk13 long ride (60km, 120 min) is already well-calibrated for this phase.

The Wk12 long run on 13 Sep (20km, 180 min) is excessive given zero running has been recorded in 4 weeks — cap it at 10–12km easy to avoid injury ahead of both the Half Oceanman swim and the Treviso 10K.

In the final 7 days before the Half Oceanman (from 27 Sep), reduce all non-swim sessions to easy maintenance only and do one final open-water 2,000m dress-rehearsal swim on ~30 Sep to build confidence in race conditions.
